title: Cap. III Rat. 10: mere beneplacitum makes works idle — Predestinati / Sigebertus
latin: Rat. 10. Si Deus non habens rationem meritorum, ex solo suo beneplacito decrevisset singulares personas, puta Paulum et Petrum, beare, cum bona opera nihil prorsus operarentur ad gloriam consequendam, Fac igitur Petrum in bonis operibus ambulare, tamen gloria non tribuetur illi ex ullo merito ad talia opera: fac eum bona opera prorsus negligere, Deus tamen virtute beneplaciti sui dabit illi gloriam destinatam: At hoc est valde absurdum, et propendet in errorem Praedestinatorum, quos Sigebertus in Chronico suo ostendit docuisse, Pie viventibus non prodesse bona opera ad gloriam, si Praedestinati non sint; flagitiose viventibus non obesse ulla scelera, si sint ex praedestinatis.
pass_a: Reason 10. If God, not having regard of merits, from his sole good pleasure had decreed to bless singular persons, for example Paul and Peter, since good works would operate nothing at all toward obtaining glory, Make therefore Peter walk in good works, yet glory will not be attributed to him from any merit toward such works: make him altogether neglect good works, God nevertheless by the force of his good pleasure will give him the destined glory: But this is very absurd, and leans toward the error of the Predestinarians, whom Sigebert in his Chronicle shows to have taught that to those living piously good works do not profit unto glory, if they be not Predestinated; to those living flagitiously no crimes harm, if they be of the predestinated.
pass_b: Rat. 10. If God, ignoring merits, had from mere good pleasure decreed to bless particular persons — say Paul and Peter — then good works would do nothing toward obtaining glory. So let Peter walk in good works: still glory is not credited to him from any desert of those works. Let him neglect good works entirely: God will still give him the destined glory by the force of his good pleasure. That is highly absurd, and leans toward the Predestinarian error Sigebert's Chronicle reports: pious living's good works do not help toward glory if one is not predestinated; flagrant living's crimes do not hurt if one is.

lemmas.lemma: ex solo beneplacito / non rationem meritorum
lemmas.gloss: mere good pleasure without regard of merits
works would do nothing toward glory

title: Cap. III Rat. 10: Valencia, Vasquez, Faustus — election must rest on foresight of works
latin: Hoc argumentum urgetur a Gregorio de Valencia. Vasques etiam eodem argumento utitur. Quinetiam antiqui Pelagiani Catholicos hoc argumento oppugnabant: Sic enim Faustus Regiensis, Praedestinatis ad vitam necessaria non erit oratio; deputatis ad mortem prodesse non poterit: in istis supervacua, in illis infirma judicabitur; lib. 1. De lib. arb. c. 4. Quod de oratione, id de caeteris omnibus bonis operibus eadem argumentandi formula concludi potuit, esse nimirum supervacua, posito antecedente et gratuito decreto electionis Divinae. Electio igitur ponenda ex praescientia operum.
pass_a: This argument is pressed by Gregory of Valencia. Vasquez also uses the same argument. Moreover the ancient Pelagians attacked the Catholics with this argument: For so Faustus of Riez, To those predestinated to life prayer will not be necessary; to those appointed to death it will not be able to profit: in these it will be judged superfluous, in those weak; book 1 On free choice chapter 4. What concerning prayer, that concerning all the rest of good works by the same formula of arguing could be concluded, namely that they are superfluous, the antecedent and gratuitous decree of the divine election having been posited. Election therefore is to be posited from foresight of works.
pass_b: Gregory of Valencia presses this; Vasquez uses it too. Even the old Pelagians turned it on the Catholics — so Faustus of Riez (De lib. arb. 1.4): for those predestined to life prayer will not be necessary; for those appointed to death it cannot help — superfluous in the one case, powerless in the other. What they say of prayer they could conclude of every other good work: superfluous once an antecedent, gratuitous decree of divine election is posited. Therefore election must be set on foresight of works.

lemmas.gloss: Valencia and Vasquez press the argument
Faustus: prayer idle if election absolute
therefore election from foresight of works

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10: consequentia nulla — end-decree includes means; harvest analogy
latin: Sol. Consequentia praedictae argumentationis plane nulla est. Nam quamvis recte statuamus decretum dandi gloriam esse gratuitum, atque esse etiam prius, secundum nostrum intelligendi modum, quam decretum dandi gratiam, aut bona opera, quia illud praestituit finem, hoc media ad finem ordinat; tamen recte negamus gratiam Dei aut opera bona, quae sunt effecta gratiae, nihil operari ad gloriae consecutionem. Ratio in promptu est: Quia quando ponimus absolutum et efficax Dei decretum de quocunque eventu futuro, intelligimus simul Deum propter hanc intentionem adimplendam velle adhibere et applicare illa media, quibus tale effectum producatur. In antecedente ergo decreto dandi gloriam, virtualiter includitur consequens decretum dandi bona opera caeteraque media quae via sunt ad regnum gloriae. Operantur itaque haec media ad finis consecutionem isto modo, licet huic personae singulari finis non fuerit destinatus ex antecedente illorum praevisione. Facito ut appositione exempli hoc magis illucescat: Sumatur Deum antecedente decreto, et gratuito praestituisse magnam frugum ubertatem anno insequente nobis donare: Si quis hinc inferat, Ergo nihil bona aeris temperies, nihil tempestivae pluviae, nihil labor agricolarum operabuntur ad hanc ubertatem efficiendam, ridicule concluserit; quia in illo priori decreto de dando fructu non excluditur voluntas exsequendi per media, sed ut ab eo dependens includitur.
pass_a: Solution. The consequence of the aforesaid argumentation is plainly none. For although we rightly establish that the decree of giving glory is gratuitous, and is also prior, according to our mode of understanding, to the decree of giving grace, or good works, because that pre-establishes the end, this orders the means to the end; yet we rightly deny that the grace of God or good works, which are effects of grace, operate nothing toward the obtaining of glory. The reason is ready: Because when we posit an absolute and efficacious decree of God concerning any future event whatever, we understand at the same time that God, for the fulfilling of this intention, wills to employ and apply those means by which such an effect is produced. In the antecedent decree therefore of giving glory, the consequent decree of giving good works and the other means which are the way to the kingdom of glory is virtually included. These means therefore operate toward the obtaining of the end in this manner, although for this singular person the end was not destined from antecedent foresight of them. Let it be done that by the addition of an example this may shine more: Let it be taken that God by an antecedent decree, and gratuitously, had pre-established to give us a great abundance of fruits in the following year: If anyone from this should infer, Therefore neither a good temper of the air, nor seasonable rains, nor the labor of farmers will operate anything toward effecting this abundance, he would conclude ridiculously; because in that prior decree of giving the fruit the will of executing through means is not excluded, but as depending from it is included.
pass_b: Sol. That argumentation's consequence is plainly none. We rightly hold the decree to give glory gratuitous, and prior (in our way of understanding) to the decree to give grace or good works — because the first sets the end, the second orders means to the end — yet we deny that God's grace or the good works that are grace's effects do nothing toward obtaining glory. The reason is ready: an absolute, efficacious decree of any future event already means God wills to employ and apply the means that produce that effect. So in the antecedent decree to give glory is virtually included the consequent decree to give good works and the other means that are the way to glory's kingdom. Those means therefore work toward obtaining the end this way, even if for this particular person the end was not destined from prior foresight of them. Take an example: suppose God by an antecedent, gratuitous decree had set to give us a great harvest next year. To infer Therefore neither fair weather, nor seasonable rains, nor farmers' labor will do anything toward that abundance is ridiculous — for in that prior decree to give the fruit the will to execute through means is not shut out but included as depending on it.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10: Bannes — no real independence; Apage — glory with future good works
latin: Idem prorsus cogitandum de absoluto et efficaci decreto quoad Petri glorificationem, et de mediis gratiae bonorumque operum per quae ad gloriam perducetur. Vide hoc doctissimus Bannes, et hujusmodi consequentias explosit: In istis consequentiis, inquit, ex prioritate nostrae rationis quantum ad modum intelligendi in uno genere causae, colligitur absque ulla apparentia prioritas realis in ipsis rebus, vel Independentia unius rei ab altera secundum ordinem statutum a Deo: sicuti quis diceret, Prius a Deo volita est forma quam materia, ergo etiamsi non esset futura materia, fieret forma. Haec ille, In 1. qu. 23. art. 2. Par illorum stultitia qui argumentantur: Si prius Petro volita sit gloria quam gratia, aut quam praevisa sunt bona opera quae fluunt ex gratia, tum etiamsi Petrus maneret expers gratiae et bonorum operum, gloriam tamen consequeretur. Apage has ineptias! Nam licet Deus non velit gloriam huic singulari homini ex intuitu antecedente operum ejus, sed ex beneplacito voluntatis suae gratuito, vult tamen illi gloriam cum intuitu bonae operationis futurae, tanquam modi necessarii, per quem ipse Deus ordinavit ut ad hunc finem obtinendum homo procederet.
pass_a: The very same is to be thought concerning the absolute and efficacious decree as to Peter's glorification, and concerning the means of grace and of good works through which he will be brought to glory. See this the most learned Báñez, and he exploded consequences of this sort: In these consequences, he says, from the priority of our reason as to the mode of understanding in one kind of cause, a real priority in the things themselves is gathered without any appearance, or the Independence of one thing from another according to the order established by God: as if someone should say, Form was willed by God prior to matter, therefore even if matter were not going to be, form would come to be. These things he, On 1. q. 23 art. 2. Equal is the folly of those who argue: If glory was willed to Peter prior to grace, or prior to the foresight of the good works which flow from grace, then even if Peter remained devoid of grace and of good works, he would nevertheless obtain glory. Away with these ineptitudes! For although God does not will glory to this singular human being from an antecedent intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, yet he wills glory to him with the intuition of future good working, as of a necessary mode, through which God himself ordained that the human being should proceed to obtaining this end.
pass_b: Think the same of the absolute, efficacious decree for Peter's glorification, and of the means of grace and good works by which he is brought to glory. Báñez saw this and exploded such consequences (In 1. q.23 a.2): from a priority in our way of understanding one kind of cause, people infer without any show a real priority in the things themselves, or independence of one from another in the order God set — as if: Form was willed by God before matter, therefore form would come to be even if matter never would. Equal folly: If glory was willed to Peter before grace, or before foresight of the good works that flow from grace, then even if Peter stayed devoid of grace and good works he would still get glory. Away with that nonsense! Though God does not will glory to this particular person from prior intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, he still wills him glory with intuition of future good working as the necessary mode by which God ordained that the person proceed to that end.

lemmas.gloss: Báñez: no real independence from mind's priority
glory willed with future good working as necessary mode

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10 close: not Predestinati — works profit; Father prepares repentance
latin: Praedestinatorum igitur haeresis nihil ad nos, qui pleno ore docemus opera pietatis prodesse ad consecutionem gloriae; Flagitia etiam praedestinatis ipsis ita obstare, ut nisi per poenitentiam et vitae novitatem abjicerentur, non possent ad regnum gloriae pervenire. Sed idem caelestis Pater, qui gratuito illis gloriam destinavit, hanc poenitentiam et vitae novitatem infallibiliter etiam iisdem praeparavit.
pass_a: The heresy of the Predestinarians therefore is nothing to us, who with full mouth teach that works of piety profit unto the obtaining of glory; and that flagitious deeds even to the predestinated themselves so stand in the way, that unless they were cast off through repentance and newness of life, they could not arrive at the kingdom of glory. But the same heavenly Father, who gratuitously destined glory to them, has also infallibly prepared for the same this repentance and newness of life.
pass_b: So the Predestinarian heresy is nothing to us — we teach outright that works of piety profit toward obtaining glory, and that crimes block even the predestinated so that, unless cast off by repentance and newness of life, they cannot reach the kingdom of glory. Yet the same heavenly Father who gratuitously destined them glory has also infallibly prepared for them that repentance and newness of life.

lemmas.gloss: works of piety profit toward glory
